blocks.text: That the kite is named from flying, דאה daa, as in Leviticus, rather than from sight, ראה raa, as in Deuteronomy.

Next comes דאה daa, or ראה raa. For it is not certain which way it should be written, since the same bird is called דאה in Leviticus and ראה raa in Deuteronomy; of these, one is taken from flying, the other from sight. For דאה daa is the verb to fly, and ראה raa to see. The letters Daleth and Resh, being very similar, are often confused by scribes. Thus דודנים Dodanim, Gen. X, 4. and רודנים Rodanim, 1 Par. I, 7. are the same; so are ריפת Riphath, Gen. X, 3. and דיפת Diphath, 1 Par. I, 6.; הדר Hadar, Gen. XXXVI, 39. and הדד Hadad, 1 Par. I, 46.; הדד־עזר Hadad-ezer, 2 Sam. VIII, 3. and הדר־עזר Hadar-ezer, 1 Par. XVIII, 3.; ההרודי Harodites, 2 Sam. XXIII, 25. and ההרורי Harorites, 1 Paral. XI, 27.; חמדן Hamdan, Gen. XXXVI, 26. and חמרן Hamran, 1 Par. I, 39. (var. 41.); דעואל Daguel, Num. I, 14. and VII, 42. and רעואל Raguel, Num. II, 14. And of God it is said in 2 Sam. XXII, 11. וירא vajera, and he appeared, instead of וידא vajeda, and he flew, Psal. XVIII, 11. In exactly the same way the same bird is called דאה daa in one place and ראה raa in another. But if that bird is truly the kite, as most of the ancient and more recent interpreters hold, among them Jerome, the Arabs, Munster, Castalio, Junius, Diodati, Buxtorf, Schindler, etc., I would rather have it written דאה daa than ראה raa, with the name derived from flying rather than from sight. For while writers on natural history observe nothing peculiar in the kite's sight, in its flight it has this first distinctive feature: with its wings almost motionless it hovers in the air longer than any other bird. Munster: רחף, It moved, namely as the kite moves in the air without moving its wings, etc. Budaeus: We have watched kites for a whole hour or more catching prey without beating their wings, etc. This the Italian fowlers call tendere, the French planare. For by raising the wing a little they take the movement of the air into the rest of the body as well, and are thus held up. Moreover, there is scarcely any bird that flies higher than the kite. Martial, book 9, Epigram 55:
Hence the rapacious kite flies almost to the highest stars.

Belon, De Avibus book 2, ch. 26: When a hawk is let loose at a kite, both are carried up into the highest air, so that they escape human sight. Budaeus in his Philologia: Neither herons nor kites, though hidden within the clouds, can escape human hands. Finally, the kite does not easily tire in flying. Hence Persius on Vectidius, Satire 4:
— he ploughs at Cures more than a kite could fly over.
Where Cornutus comments: As is commonly said in the proverb, "As far as kites do not fly", because kites fly a great deal. And Juvenal, Satire 9:
[II, 778] — — for whom are you keeping so many mountains, so many Apulian estates, so many kites wearied within your pastures?
